extracted.intended_audience: improvisers and improv teachers (performers, workshop leaders)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidelines for creating and playing improv characters, using mime/physicality, and selecting/structuring improv games for performance and teaching. Covers character-building, stakes, mime mechanics, game rules, and coaching/audience considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give concrete physical instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid vague emotional directives (e.g. don’t tell someone simply to ‘be sexy’).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use specific, actionable physical directions the performer can follow (e.g. “Cross your legs, tilt your chin up, smoke a cigarette and blow smoke rings”) so the actor achieves the intended physicality and feeling. This is preferable to abstract prompts which are hard to execute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a name and first line to establish character
rubrics_metrics.description: Give the character an identity and voice immediately so they can inhabit it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have the performer state a simple line (e.g. “My name’s Violet”) in the chosen voice/physicality to anchor the audience and performer. Small naming/voicing choices help ownership and immediate clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mix characters through different relationships and contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: After creating characters as strangers, move them into interactions with friends, family and lovers to reveal new dimensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage sequences where the same character meets different people (e.g. femme fatale visits her father, vulnerable old man meets grandson) so improvisers can show new emotional states and deepen the role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have others play created characters to increase ownership and variety
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask improvisers to play someone else’s character to test whether the character is distinct and transferable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reveals which elements define the character and how different performers (gender, physicality) change it — a useful exercise to build a small repertoire of characters each player ‘owns’.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commit fully — sell the character (commitment is two-thirds of your job)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you don’t sell it, the audience won’t buy it; when feeling silly, push forward rather than pull back.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Act as if you truly are the character (even if you don’t believe you’re a Vietnam veteran with a limp, act as though you are). Increasing commitment increases audience buy-in and emotional impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create dimension through surface/inside contrast
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters are more interesting when their appearance suggests the opposite of their interior (e.g. Bond looks like a playboy but is a killing machine).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce small elements that imply contradictory interior life so the audience anticipates depth; in long-form shows you can reveal softer or hidden sides over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Add an opposite or arbitrary element to hint at depth
rubrics_metrics.description: You don’t need to rewrite a character; add one novel element (an opposite or arbitrary trait) to promise dimension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a nun putting on a rosary and a gun; a cop buying flowers. These single elements raise questions and make characters richer if justified/explored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Answer the audience’s questions (useable mystery)
rubrics_metrics.description: When you arouse audience curiosity (e.g. why is a cop buying flowers?), provide payoffs or exploration so they feel satisfied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think ahead about what questions your action will pose and how you might answer them in the scene; letting the audience’s questions remain unresolved risks frustration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define what the character wants and link stakes to emotional cost
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask: what does the character want and what are the consequences of not getting it? Stakes should be tied to the character’s emotional cost, not abstract outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose goals that are rational/irrational/extreme/opposite/arbitrary to create comedy or drama (examples provided). If the audience can’t emotionally connect to the stakes, they won’t care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the price of success as well as failure
rubrics_metrics.description: Good storytelling often makes success costly — what will the character lose if they get what they want?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ‘be careful what you wish for’ outcomes (e.g. Macbeth) as improv possibilities; cost-of-success can create satisfying change and emotional payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use stakes and emotional change to make scenes worth watching
rubrics_metrics.description: Scenes should change a character in some way so the audience feels the time was spent meaningfully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design consequences (loss, revelation, transformation) so even comedic outcomes create character change (e.g. student wins test but loses potential romantic connection).

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop complementary non-improv skills (mime, impressions, juggling etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Improv benefits from a broad toolkit; physical skills and other performance abilities expand options on stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage performers to take acting or other classes and to maintain skills (even if rare in performance) because they enrich character work and make physical offers more convincing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a rich platform/props to reveal character and inspire trouble
rubrics_metrics.description: Platforms (settings, detailed props) make finding interesting trouble easier and help reveal character traits visually/physically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even minimal props (four chairs, drapes) can work if performers are good mimes; when possible, provide toys/props to inspire imaginative offers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take your time — slow, deliberate physicality is more interesting
rubrics_metrics.description: Slowness and detail in physical work engage the audience and give improvisers focus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use slow-motion scenes and deliberate pacing to deepen attention; slow mime can transfix audiences and provide breathing space after high-energy scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain spatial consistency and remember fixed points
rubrics_metrics.description: Mime objects only exist while you touch them; keep objects/doors/fridge locations consistent across performers and moments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use stage marks/tape/scratches as reference points. Exercises (shelf fixed points) train memory; each performer must respect previously established object locations to avoid breaking the illusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use ‘popping’ and discrete movements to sell object interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce small, sudden muscular actions (‘pops’) at contact points to make mime interactions feel solid and precise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Popping helps mark action endpoints, prevents overlapping motions, and emphasizes when objects meet. Beware overdoing it (creates a robotic effect). Use popping to make mime objects feel ‘sticky’ and to improve clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Add appropriate aural components to mime
rubrics_metrics.description: Mime benefits from simple noises (grunts, impact sounds) which enrich the physical world and sell the illusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage performers to make childish-sounding noises (e.g. “shtooom!”) when objects hit the floor — audiences love the added layer and it helps the world feel complete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be pedantic about mime detail and handovers
rubrics_metrics.description: Small errors (dropping, cloning) break the mime world; insist on precise object handling and continuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises: circle table with items; performers must open/use/hand over items convincingly. Correct tiny mistakes (camera opening, picture developing). Ensure handovers are clean — dropping or premature release destroys the illusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust group size for mime practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Mime exercises are best in groups of 8–10 so people perform frequently and avoid long waits that encourage cleverness-over-clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Split large groups (>12) into circles to keep engagement high and reduce audience-watching time that leads to overthinking and bad habits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select games with purpose; don’t just play lists
rubrics_metrics.description: Pick games that serve a particular teaching or performance aim rather than assembling many games indiscriminately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand the point of each game (e.g. economy, listening, platform building) and choose games that target those skills. Avoid treating games as filler.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three Word Sentences — strict rule set for a useful constraint
rubrics_metrics.description: Every utterance must be exactly three words, a complete sentence, contractions count as one word, no tailing off or grammar-mangling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This constraint forces economy, makes every word count, speeds scenes into the future, prevents repetition and cliché. Coaches may prompt beginners; use as a dramatic tool (silences become compelling).

rubrics_metrics.name: Define failure handling for games explicitly
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide ahead what happens when an improviser breaks a game constraint (options include retake, substitution, losing a life, ending scene, token punishment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different penalties have different effects — avoid destructive or humiliating punishments (wet sponges) that trivialize the game. Choose rules that preserve dignity and the desired energy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain game rules clearly to the audience (coach-as-MC role)
rubrics_metrics.description: As host/coach you must succinctly describe the game so the audience can appreciate it; avoid meaningless game names without explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare short clear explanations of procedures. Good MCing reduces audience confusion and improves the effect of the game in performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide audience vs judge enforcement for infractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether the audience should spot errors or whether the host/judge will enforce rules; this affects game dynamics and audience behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use audience policing only when it enhances fun (e.g. hissing in No S), but be careful: asking audiences to punish judges or players can undermine authority and seriousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-complexifying games (‘complexing-up’)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding unnecessary layers (e.g. X Word Sentences with wildly varying counts) can swamp story and turn the exercise into counting-ability rather than storytelling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware iterative escalation of difficulty that shifts attention from story to executing the gimmick; if the game distracts from narrative variety it will be abandoned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Questions Only — strict expectations and pairing recommendation
rubrics_metrics.description: Players may only speak in legitimate single-sentence questions (no non-question taglines or fragments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the restriction is difficult, start in pairs and enforce strictness (strike and retake non-questions). The game often stalls larger groups; set expectations accordingly.
